question.text:
A family of pairwise disjoint Lebesgue-measurable subsets of [0, 1] has strictly positive measure
for every member. What is the largest possible cardinality of this family?
(A) One.
(B) Any finite cardinality, but never infinite.
(C) Countably infinite.
(D) The cardinality of R.
(E) Greater than the cardinality of R.

solution.text:
For each positive integer k, at most k disjoint members can have measure at least 1/k,
since their measures sum to at most one. Every positive-measure member belongs to one
of these finite families for sufficiently large k, so the whole family is countable. Countably

(A) C is countable and has measure zero.
(B) C is uncountable and has measure zero.
(C) C is uncountable and has measure 1/3.
(D) C is finite and nonempty.
(E) C is not measurable.

question.text:
If A, B are measurable, m(A) = m(B) = 1, and m(A△B) = 0, what is m(A ∩ B)?
(A) 0
(B) It cannot be determined
(C) 2
(D) 1/2
(E) 1

solution.text:
The symmetric difference consists of the disjoint sets A \ B and B \ A. Both have measure
zero, so removing A \ B from A leaves intersection measure one.
